experiments.notes: Male-specific effect: no significant effect on female survival at 14.4 ppm (pooled or per site); female arm not recorded separately because the female result is a null at every endpoint. Site-specific median increases 26/9/23% (TJL/UM/UT), all P < 0.003. Authors note the mechanism of male specificity is unknown; 14.4 ppm dose was uterotrophic in ovariectomized mice, so female null is not due to lack of bioavailability. Sex quote documents the male-only nature of the effect.

type.source_quote: Nordihydroguaiaretic (NDGA) is produced by the leaves of the creosote bush (Larrea tridentata). It is both a lipoxygenase inhibitor and potent antioxidant.

agent.source_quote: we tested the effects of NDGA at 800, 2500, and 5000 ppm in males and at 5000 ppm in females

dose.value: 2500 ppm (reference dose; 800 and 5000 ppm also tested)
dose.source_quote: we tested the effects of NDGA at 800, 2500, and 5000 ppm in males and at 5000 ppm in females

age_at_start.source_quote: NDGA was purchased from Cayman Chemicals (Ann Arbor, MI, USA) and mixed at a concentration of either 800, 2500, or 5000 ppm and fed to male mice beginning at 4 months of age.

direction.source_quote: NDGA increased survival of male mice at each of the doses tested, with increases in median lifespan at each dose

median_change_pct.source_quote: NDGA (2500): n=133, median 851 days, +10%, P=0.015 (Table 2, males pooled)

p_value.source_quote: NDGA (2500): n=133, median 851 days, +10%, P=0.015 (Table 2, males pooled)

experiments.notes: One record for the reference dose (2500 ppm); all three doses significant in males (800 ppm +6% P=0.023, 2500 ppm +10% P=0.015, 5000 ppm +9% P=0.003). No effect on maximal lifespan at any dose in males, and no effect in females at 5000 ppm despite blood levels matching males at 2500 ppm - max_change_pct left null because no significant max effect exists. Internal inconsistency in the paper: the introduction says treatment started at 6 months, the methods say 4 months; methods value recorded with medium confidence. Good extractor stress case.

Dose escalated mid-study (600 to 1200 ppm at 17 months) because 600 ppm did not modulate xenobiotic-response liver mRNA - unusual protocol worth an extractor test.

mechanism.source_quote: Rapamycin (Rapa) and Met each inhibit mTORC1, but through distinct mechanisms. In addition, Rapa affects glucose tolerance through inhibition of a second mTOR complex, mTORC2, resulting in hepatic insulin resistance (Lamming et al. 2013), while Met acts to activate AMPK, suppressing hepatic glucose output

direction.source_quote: this combination led to a 23% increase in survival compared with controls in both sexes, as well as to significant increases in maximum lifespan (P < 0.001)

median_change_pct.source_quote: this combination led to a 23% increase in survival compared with controls in both sexes, as well as to significant increases in maximum lifespan (P < 0.001)

p_value.source_quote: this combination led to a 23% increase in survival compared with controls in both sexes, as well as to significant increases in maximum lifespan (P < 0.001)

experiments.notes: Median +23% identical in both sexes, so recorded as one mixed record rather than a male/female split. Max lifespan significantly increased in both sexes but with different magnitudes (90th percentile +10% males, +17% females) - left null at record level, per-sex values here. sample_size 300 is the sum of the two sex arms (158 M + 142 F), medium confidence. The added benefit over rapamycin alone is a historical comparison (P=0.12 site-stratified, P=0.049 unstratified) - suggestive, not conclusive, per the authors.

type.source_quote: Metformin (Met) is an oral antidiabetic drug that has been FDA-approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes

agent.source_quote: Beginning at 9 months of age, groups of male and female mice began consuming a diet containing 1000 ppm (0.1%) Met.

dose.source_quote: Beginning at 9 months of age, groups of male and female mice began consuming a diet containing 1000 ppm (0.1%) Met.

age_at_start.source_quote: Beginning at 9 months of age, groups of male and female mice began consuming a diet containing 1000 ppm (0.1%) Met.

direction.source_quote: Met led to a 7% increase in median lifespan of males when data were pooled across sites, but the effect was not statistically significant (P = 0.35).

experiments.notes: Designated no_effect hard case: a nominal +7% male median (P=0.35) must not be coerced into increase. Numeric changes deliberately null because no endpoint was significant; per-sex nominal values (males +7% P=0.35, females 0% P=0.79) kept here. Direct cross-paper disagreement with Martin-Montalvo 2013 (10.1038/ncomms3192): same agent, same 0.1% dose, positive there in C57BL/6 males (Gehan-Breslow) vs null here in UM-HET3 with log-rank and larger n - the authors discuss the statistical and design differences explicitly. Flagship contradiction-detection case.

direction.source_quote: Pooling across sites, there were no significant effects at either dose of FO on survival of male or female mice.

experiments.notes: Both doses null in both sexes (pooled); one record covering both doses since neither reached significance. Site-level heterogeneity worth noting: high dose decreased male longevity at UM (-18%, P=0.003) while the low dose trended up at UT (+9%, P=0.06) - the authors use this to argue for multi-site testing. Body weight increased dose-dependently in males, so the agent was biologically active.
